To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

mast cells (MCs), best known for their contributions in IgE-dependent allergic disorders, also can perform effector and immunomodulatory roles that contribute both to homeostasis and pathology in mucosal sites.

mast cells can be activated by diverse stimuli to express functional programs that contribute to homeo- stasis or pathology in the mucosal tissues of the lung, gastrointestinal tract, reproductive tract, skin, and other tissues.
mast cells (MCs), which reside in mucosal and other tissues, are activated in response to diverse signals, including those derived from the external and internal environments.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (a) What is the nature of the MCs that populate mucosal tissues?
understanding the mechanisms by which MCs are activated and function in mucosal tissues during health and disease.
understanding how MCs contribute to mucosal immunity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the functional roles of MCs in mucosal immunity remain largely unknown, and that much remains to be learned about the roles played by these cells in mucosal immune responses.
MCs are not just effector cells, and that they can be immunoregulatory cells, but that they are not always immunoregulatory, and that they are not only effector cells.
MCs can participate in both protective and pathologic processes in mucosal tissues and that they can be activated to perform both pro- and anti-inflammatory functions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the MCs are a versatile cell type that can be activated to perform multiple functions in mucosal immunity and that their functional repertoire may be expanded by the expression of additional receptors, cytokines, and other mediators.

MCs can be activated to perform a variety of effector and immunomodulatory functions in mucosal tissues and that the balance between these activities is critical in determining the overall outcome of an immune response in these sites.
MCs are not only effector cells, but they also can be activated as immunoregulatory cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
MCs have the potential to perform a broad range of functions in mucosal tissues and that their contributions are dependent on the context in which they are activated.

, although MCs can mediate IgE-dependent effector and immunomodulatory functions, these cells are not limited to this role and, indeed, may have a more diverse role in mucosal immunity than previously appreciated.

MCs can be activated to contribute to host defense in diverse mucosal sites, including those that are not usually considered to be “immune” in nature, and that they are capable of performing diverse effector functions that are relevant to the host’s defense against pathogens and/or the regulation of immune responses.
